title: Pass a booking on, and an illegal working penalty can now land on you as the employer
seo_title: Right to work checks now cover individual sub-contractors
dek: Since 1 October, the UK's illegal working rules reach individual sub-contractors and people on worker's contracts. For the civil penalty, anyone contracted to provide or arrange work who passes it on is treated as employing whoever personally does any of it. What that means for crew bookings.
summary: Since 1 October 2026, UK right to work checks cover worker's contracts and individual sub-contractors, and penalty liability can run up a contract chain.
body:
Since 1 October, the UK's illegal working rules no longer stop at the payroll. [Section 48](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2025/31/section/48) of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025, switched on that day by [S.I. 2026/683](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2026/683), inserts new sections 14A and 15A into the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006. For sections 15 to 24 of that Act, "employing" someone now includes engaging an individual under a worker's contract, or engaging them as an individual sub-contractor. Online matching services are in as well: providing the details of an individual service provider to potential clients or customers counts.

The explanatory note to the commencement regulations says as much: the change extends the illegal working provisions in sections 15 to 24 to arrangements beyond contracts of employment, and it "expands liability for civil penalties under section 15".

Then there is section 15A, which is the bit that should make production offices sit up. It has two triggers. The first is a person who "employs an individual to provide work or services", and read with section 14A that now takes in workers and individual sub-contractors. The second is a person who "is contracted to provide, or arrange for the provision of, work or services" and enters a contract under which someone else is to provide or arrange the work, or part of it. Either way, for the purposes of the civil penalty in [section 15](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2006/13/section/15), that person "is to be treated as employing" any individual who personally provides the work "(or any part of the work or services)". That holds where it has no contract with the individual, and where it does not even know they are the one doing it. And for anyone contracted to provide or arrange the work, it applies "regardless of whether that contract is the first or any other contract in a chain of contracts".

There is a limit. Section 15A(7) carries that deeming into sections 15, 16, 17, 23 and 24 of the 2006 Act and no further, so it does not reach sections 18 to 22. Section 14A's wider meaning of employing does run across all of sections 15 to 24.

## What that looks like on a job

Events run on chains. A client hires an agency, the agency hires a production company, the production company hires an AV supplier, and the AV supplier rings a crew chief, who rings the people they trust.

Section 14A(3) defines an individual sub-contractor as an individual who has a contract with person B to provide work or services, where person B has contracted with a third party "to provide, or arrange for the provision of" that work and the individual has not. Hold that up against a typical crew booking and it describes a lot of us. A phone call is enough, too: for these sections a contract now includes one that is "express or implied and (if it is express) whether oral or in writing".

Section 15A is the one that runs uphill. Anyone in that chain who was contracted to deliver or arrange the work and passed it, or part of it, on is treated as employing the person who actually turns up with the cable reel. On our reading, that includes the crew chief who took a booking for four and filled three of the slots with mates. If that is you, you are not just the freelancer in this story. For the penalty, you are the employer as well.

Our reading of the client end: the chain rule in section 15A turns on being contracted to provide or arrange the work, and a corporate client buying a finished event is usually not contracted to anyone to do either. No source we read deals with that case, so treat it as our reading, not a safe harbour.

A client that engages an individual directly is a different question. Section 14A(1)(a) covers engaging someone on a worker's contract, but section 14A(3) only counts a contract as one where the engager "is neither a client nor customer of any profession or business undertaking carried on by" the individual. Book a freelancer's own business as its customer and you are outside that limb. The individual sub-contractor limb has no such exclusion, so, as we read it, a freelancer booked by a supplier who is itself contracted for the job is in either way.

## What the Home Office expects

The Home Office updated its [employer's guide](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/right-to-work-checks-employers-guide) and its [right to work checklist](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/right-to-work-checklist/employers-right-to-work-checklist-accessible-version) on 1 October. The checklist says a prescribed right to work check must be carried out before the worker starts, for a worker engaged under a worker's contract and for one engaged as an individual sub-contractor.

It also asks a question every freelancer will recognise: "Does the contractual arrangement permit substitution?" Where it does, the checklist's answer is: "Any substitute undergoes a prescribed right to work check before starting work or providing services." The old habit of sending a mate when you have double-booked now comes with paperwork attached.

Substitution is not a trigger in sections 14A or 15A; the word appears in neither. It turns up in the checklist as a screening question, and as part of the defence. The Act gets to substitutes anyway, on our reading: if you engage someone and they send a mate, the first trigger in section 15A treats you as employing the mate.

That defence, the statutory excuse against extended liability, has three parts in the checklist: a written statement containing the prescribed contractual terms and conditions, substitution controls where they apply, and identity verification. The excuse itself sits in section 15(3) of the 2006 Act: an employer "is excused from paying a penalty if he shows that he complied with any prescribed requirements in relation to the employment". Section 15(4) takes it away from an employer who knew the employment was contrary to the section. We have not traced the order that prescribes those requirements for the new arrangements.

## The penalty, and the code

On penalties, the roofing trade body [NFRC](https://www.nfrc.co.uk/resource/right-to-work-checks.html) put it like this on 9 October: "A business may face a civil penalty of up to £60,000 for each illegal worker." That is the trade body's figure, and we have not confirmed it. Section 15(2) lets the Secretary of State require "a penalty of a specified amount not exceeding the prescribed maximum", and that maximum is set outside the Act, in an instrument we did not trace for this piece.

The Home Office's [code of practice](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/illegal-working-penalties-codes-of-practice-for-employers), now dated 1 October 2026 with "draft" removed from its title, covers the factors the Home Office takes into account when it sets the amount of a penalty. Its GOV.UK page records no change to penalty amounts on 1 October; a note from 22 February 2024 says the changes to civil penalties were "already in force with the new amounts". We could not read the code's own figures for this piece. Be wary of anyone quoting precise starting points at you without a page number.

## Our view

It is tempting to read all this as IR35 by the back door. [Roots Contractor Insurance](https://rootsinsurance.co.uk/right-to-work-checks-contractors-october-2026/), a contractor insurance broker, argues it is not: in its view the change does not turn every limited company contractor into an employee, and right to work sits apart from IR35. We agree. As we read them, the new sections decide who has to check and who can be fined, not anyone's employment status for tax or employment rights. The wording does blur it: section 14A(2) says references in sections 15 to 24 to an employer include the person doing the engaging, and references to an employee include the individual. That is our reading, not a ruling, and none of the legislation or Home Office pages we read mentions IR35.

Roots also says identity and right to work compliance may become a more visible part of onboarding. Our own guess is that share code requests start arriving with booking confirmations, and that crew terms grow a clause about substitutes and onward subcontracting.

NFRC tells its members to review their existing arrangements rather than assume their current checks and contracts are sufficient, and expects the risk to be greatest for those with more complex labour arrangements. An event supply chain four or five contracts deep, with a crew chief's group chat at the bottom of it, is about as complex as they come.

confirmed.text: Section 48 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 inserts sections 14A and 15A into the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006. Under 14A(1), employing in sections 15 to 24 includes engaging an individual on a worker's contract or as an individual sub-contractor, and an online matching service providing a service provider's details to potential clients or customers.

Section 14A(3) defines an individual sub-contractor as an individual who has a contract with person B to provide work or services, where person B has contracted with a third party to provide, or arrange for the provision of, the work or services and the individual has not.

Section 14A(3) defines a worker's contract so that it applies only where the person engaging the individual is neither a client nor customer of any profession or business undertaking carried on by that individual.

Under section 15A(1) and (4), a person who employs an individual to provide work or services, or who is contracted to provide, or arrange for the provision of, work or services and contracts with another person to provide or arrange it (or part of it), is to be treated for the purposes of section 15 as employing any individual who personally provides the work or any part of it.

Section 15A(4) and (5) apply that deeming where there is no contract with the individual or no knowledge that they are doing the work, and whether the contract is the first or any other in a chain of contracts; section 15A(7) carries it into sections 15, 16, 17, 23 and 24 only.

S.I. 2026/683, made on 24 June 2026, brings section 48 into force on 1 October 2026. Its explanatory note says section 48 extends sections 15 to 24 of the 2006 Act to arrangements beyond contracts of employment and expands liability for civil penalties under section 15.

Section 15 of the 2006 Act allows a penalty of a specified amount not exceeding the prescribed maximum, and excuses an employer who shows it complied with any prescribed requirements, unless it knew the employment was contrary to the section.
The Home Office employer's guide to right to work checks was last updated on 1 October 2026.
The Home Office checklist says a prescribed right to work check must be carried out before the worker starts for a worker's contract and for an individual sub-contractor.
The checklist asks whether the contractual arrangement permits substitution, and where it does, expects any substitute to undergo a prescribed right to work check before starting.

The checklist lists three parts of the statutory excuse against extended liability: a written statement with the prescribed contractual terms, substitution controls where applicable, and identity verification.
The code of practice is listed on GOV.UK as dated 1 October 2026, with 'draft' removed from its title, and covers the factors the Home Office takes into account when setting the amount of a penalty.

impact:
**Freelance crew.** The check has to happen before you start, so expect it before your first day on a new booking rather than on the morning of the show. If you hold an eVisa, the Home Office checklist says the online service must be used, with a share code and your date of birth, so know how to generate one. The other routes are a manual document check or a check through a digital verification service provider, which the checklist says "is not mandated". A clipped passport is not acceptable proof.

**Sending a substitute.** If your terms allow it, the substitute needs a prescribed check before they start. Tell the booker days ahead, not from the car park.

**Crew chiefs who book their own team.** If you take a booking and hand parts of it to others, section 15A treats you as employing whoever personally does any part of the work, for the purposes of the civil penalty. Your way out is the statutory excuse, so check them before they start and keep the record. Put the terms in writing too.

**Production companies and AV suppliers (and the agencies above them).** Map your chains, job by job. Section 15A covers anyone contracted to "arrange for the provision of" work who passes it on, so an agency that never touches a flight case is in the chain as well. Where workers come to you through another employer or a matching platform, the Home Office expects a written statement with the prescribed contract terms to be in place before work starts. On the day, identity verification has to confirm that "the individual carrying out the work or services is the same individual" who was checked. In our view that makes it a job for whoever runs sign-in at crew call.

**Records.** Keep copies "for the duration of employment and for 2 years afterwards", and record the date the check was made. The Home Office is blunt about it: "Simply writing a date on the copy document on its own will not be sufficient."

**Before you redraft any contract,** read the code of practice and the full employer's guide. The checklist only says the written statement must contain "the prescribed contractual terms and conditions"; it does not list them.
verdict_note: In force since 1 October. If you book people who book people, get the check and the substitute rule in place before the next job, with paperwork to prove both. Read the code of practice before you rewrite a single clause.
